summary: Federated identity is usually tied to web services, but interest is growing in non-web uses. This informational RFC documents a selection of such contexts whose user experience could improve using technologies based on the ABFAB architecture.

eli5.summary: A list of everyday situations beyond websites where one shared login would make life easier.

questions: why use federated identity for non-web services
how does federated authentication help hpc systems
subtitle: Federated identity for non-web applications and services.

tldr.problem: Most organizations use federated identity systems for web services, but many non-web applications and services lack standard ways to authenticate users across organizational boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents real-world scenarios where ABFAB (Application Bridging for Federated Access Beyond Web) technology could enable federated authentication for cloud services, computing systems, databases, printing, and IoT devices.
tldr.outcome: The document establishes use cases to guide the development of ABFAB protocols that extend federated identity beyond web-only systems, improving user experience and reducing operational overhead.

today: RFC 7832 documents requirements and scenarios driving the ABFAB effort. It remains informational and has not been obsoleted, so it continues to serve as the reference for non-web federated identity use cases in the IETF.

sections.title: Federated Identity Beyond the Web
sections.content:
Federated identity is normally tied to web-based services. When you log into a university's email from home, or use your company account to access a vendor's web portal, you are using federated authentication. The RFC starts with the observation that this same technology could benefit many non-web services, yet most protocols outside the web ecosystem lack standard ways to do it.

Federated identity means sharing identity and authentication information across organizational boundaries without each organization having to maintain its own separate user database. One sign-on at your home organization, then seamless access to services elsewhere. The RFC, published in May 2016, documents how this could work for cloud applications, scientific computing, network infrastructure, databases, printing, media streaming, and even IoT devices.
sections.eli5: Right now, you might have one login for your work email, another for the company's file storage, a third for the cloud printer, and more. Federated identity means using the same login everywhere, like how you log into a website using your Google or Facebook account.

sections.title: Why Non-Web Services Matter
sections.content:
The RFC notes that organizations increasingly use cloud services, but many cloud applications are not accessed through web browsers. For example, an accountant might use a desktop email client (SMTP, IMAP, or POP) to access cloud email, not a web mail interface. A scientist might connect to a supercomputer via SSH, or a nurse might access medical records through a legacy database client.

Today, organizations handle this in two problematic ways: they either synchronize credentials from their identity system to the cloud provider (costly and risky for privacy), or they provision accounts directly with each service. With many services, this overhead becomes untenable. ABFAB technology could solve this by allowing federated authentication to work with any protocol, not just HTTP.
sections.eli5: Imagine needing to give an accountant a separate password for the desktop email app, the file server, the scanner, and the expense system, instead of using the same login everywhere. ABFAB would let organizations use one login for all of it.

sections.title: The Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC enumerates nine major areas where federated identity would improve user experience:

Cloud Services covers software as a service (SaaS like email or CRM), platforms as a service (PaaS like databases), and infrastructure as a service (IaaS like virtual machines). Desktop applications connecting to cloud services without authenticating through a web page are the focus.

High-Performance Computing (HPC) serves scientific researchers. HPC centers currently issue digital certificates or manually provisioned accounts; federated identity would let scientists use their university login to submit jobs to supercomputers anywhere, and enable workloads to move between centers without credential overhead.

Grid Infrastructure is similar but for distributed computing across independent organizations. Users in Virtual Organizations would use federated credentials instead of managing X.509 certificates.

Databases and Directories are crucial for storing student records, project data, and identity information. External users (auditors, visiting researchers, cross-organizational teams) currently need manually provisioned access; federated authentication would eliminate that administrative burden.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows nine real scenarios: a scientist logging into a supercomputer with her university account; a nurse accessing patient records at a visiting hospital; an auditor viewing student records across schools; a cloud service accepting login tokens from your employer.

sections.title: More Applications: Media, Printing, and Devices
sections.content:
Media Streaming services often restrict content with digital rights controls. Federated authentication allows a media service to grant access to specific users without having to manage their credentials itself.

Printing is a simple but practical example: a visiting researcher from another university should be able to print to campus printers without needing a temporary account. ABFAB would enable the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) to accept federated credentials.

Telecoms Infrastructure presents a novel case. A mobile network operator could use ABFAB to let users of its network authenticate to applications and services using their operator-issued identity, without having to configure credentials on their device.

Smart Objects and IoT devices add another dimension. A smart power meter, a camera, or an autonomous vehicle might authenticate itself to cloud services via an identity provider, delegating authorization decisions to the provider instead of having to implement complex security logic on the device itself.

S/MIME Security Services use policy decision points and attribute providers to enforce access control on encrypted email. ABFAB could supply the authentication and attribute exchange that such a system needs.
sections.eli5: A visitor can print at another university without a temporary account. A smart thermostat talks to a utility company's energy service using a central identity server. A drone authenticates to cloud services via the manufacturer's identity provider.

sections.title: Security and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC is purely informational: it documents use cases, not protocols. It does not define ABFAB technologies itself; that comes from the ABFAB architecture specification (RFC 7831). The RFC notes that security considerations for the architecture are documented in RFC 7831, and protocols that implement ABFAB must follow their own security requirements.

One key assumption the RFC makes explicit: it assumes that any pre-provisioning of accounts (mapping a federated identity to an application's account) happens before ABFAB comes into play. That out-of-band step is outside the scope; ABFAB handles the authentication part once accounts exist.
sections.eli5: This document is a list of ideas, not a blueprint. It assumes someone has already set up which users are allowed to access which services. ABFAB then handles checking that you are who you say you are.
